problem: Existing indoor world generators either give perceptually realistic but physically unsound scenes, or simulable but domain-generic layouts (mostly sanitized residential from 3D-FRONT) with fixed asset databases and no robot-operational constraints.
motivation: Social-robot training and validation needs simulation environments that follow the legal, spatial and object conventions of the target domain (hospital, office, residential), including robot infrastructure such as charging docks and corridor widths. Such knowledge is domain-specific and not captured by generic priors, so it must be retrieved and used to ground generation.
key_idea: An LLM domain agent autonomously builds a provenance-tracked domain knowledge database via grounded web search, which a RAG pipeline then uses to generate floorplans and asset placements, exported as simulator-ready worlds for Isaac Sim and Gazebo.
insight: Grounding generation in retrieved standards (including robot-specific constraints) lets one pipeline cover multiple domains and yields denser, better-spaced object layouts than baselines in the paper's single comparison (Table 3, residential prompts only). The evidence is thin: n=18 per method, Gemini-judged perceptual metrics, and no ablation of the RAG component.
method: Domain Database generation: a 4-stage LLM pipeline (domain/country inference, Gemini+Google Search grounded research over 8 topics x k=2 passes, corpus structuring/deduplication, deterministic synthesis) yields a schema-validated database of constraints with provenance (URL, publisher, jurisdiction, confidence).

Robot infrastructure constraints: topic (h) retrieves robot placement, charging, circulation and docking rules (e.g. dock clearance >=1.2 m, corridor >=1.8 m for bidirectional traffic) that are injected into generation prompts.

Constraint retrieval: room-type keywords from the scene graph classify the building type; all matching references are rendered as natural-language bullets in the LLM prompt under 'Reference Room Size Standards'.

Asset database: 259 annotated 3D assets (139 office, 71 hospital, 49 residential; mainly USDZ) with bounding box, materials, colors, HOI affordances, face direction, tags and description, embedded as text for nearest-neighbor natural-language retrieval.

Text-to-Graph: an LLM with few-shot examples turns the prompt into a scene graph of rooms (with 8-15 asset names each) and adjacency/door edges, plus robot-operation zones (cleaning_zone, service_zone, charging_buffer).
Floorplan generation: a RAG-conditioned LLM outputs room and door polygons; post-processing with Shapely derives walls and assigns materials to build a WorldDescription.

Asset population: multi-stage asset retrieval and ranking, LLM placement proposals validated by hard constraints (no overlap, room bounds, wall offsets) with a position-search fallback, then export to world.yaml (with a scenario generation stage for spotlight/ambient agents).

setting.backbone: Gemini (frozen, with Google Search grounding) for research and generation; text embedding for asset retrieval
setting.training_data: none (training-free; LLM prompting + RAG over an auto-generated domain database and a 259-asset database)
setting.observation: text prompt plus domain label, jurisdiction tag and optional scene graph (world generation, not an agent navigation policy)
setting.action_space: not applicable (generates 3D worlds; outputs floorplan polygons and object poses)

numbers_note: No navigation benchmark results; the paper evaluates world generation quality (Layout-FID, object counts, Gemini-based ratings) on 18 residential worlds per method, which do not fit the canonical benchmark list.
results: On 18 residential worlds per method, D3D-GEN has the highest object count (54.56), objects per room (7.06), object spacing (9.19 m), Visual score (7.61), VQA accuracy (0.400) and Scene Rating (8.63). It beats DiffuScene on those metrics, though DiffuScene has a better Layout-FID (2531.05 vs 5377.19) and Holodeck a higher Layout score (8.46 vs 8.33). It also generated 450 worlds across residential, office and hospital domains, always matching the requested room count.
limitations: Depends on an existing asset database (259 assets), which may not be available for every domain; the domain database can only be generated once from the prompt and cannot be edited interactively.

Evaluation is thin: only n=18 residential worlds for the baseline comparison, LLM-based (Gemini) perceptual metrics, no ablations, no downstream robot navigation or social-navigation training results.
Domain coverage is limited to three domains (residential, office, hospital) and the domain classifier is fixed to those.
